body_markdown:
*Adam* writes:


I have a discussion topic for a Piston Slap: *Don’t forget your non-automotive friends when it comes to common, simple automotive projects.*


While rotating my tires the other day, I measured the brake pads[on my Buick](https://www.hagerty.com/media/advice/piston-slap/piston-slap-this-sabre-rages-against-a-throw-away-society/) and realized they are down to 2mm front and rear. Time for a brake job! I started ordering pads, rotors, etc. I mentioned in passing to my boss that I needed to do a brake job, and since the parts were somewhat expensive, I was going to do the job myself.


My boss stuck his hand up and said, “I’ve never done brakes before. Can I help?”


That gave me the idea to reach out to my non-automotive friends and family to let them know I’ll be holding a “Brake Job” class. I now have several fathers, sons, and friends showing up. I figured I could put two people on each corner, wander around, and show them what to do. Now, if we can get through the day without anyone breaking anything, and I can stop the car when we finish, it will be a win.


This reminds me, though: when we have simple jobs like this, we should attempt to share our knowledge. Even if it’s never used, at least they’ll know what it takes to get the job done.


*Sajeev* answers:


Agreed, because even if they never turn a wrench again, they will have more knowledge when scouting for/working with a local mechanic to do this work in the future! But there’s another good reason to get your friends interested in auto maintenance and repair:[Right-to-Repair laws](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/17/right-to-repair-laws) are flourishing around the country. And they could use even more cheerleading from “activated” automobile owners, in my book.


We see Right to Repair unfolding with farm equipment, smartphones, and laptops, but less so with automobiles. Or at least it feels that way in popular culture, because cars don’t occupy the same place in our hearts as equipment for our farmers, or technology we touch for hours every day. It’s both expected and easy to outsource automobile repairs or maintenance, and[it’s been that way](https://www.hagerty.com/media/hagerty-community/according-to-you-service-station-stories/) for decades.


But we can save money with DIY car repairs, and more folks would have extra wiggle room in their budget these days if they partook in the procedures. There’s only one problem, and it doesn’t involve hand tools.


So many vehicles made in the last 20 years need more than just new pads, rotors, shoes, and drums to complete a brake job. Something like the video above is needed to reset the Pad Life Monitor, lest you get stuck with an annoying warning every time the vehicle is driven. It’s doubly important if you have vehicle inspections in your area; the tech can fail you for a light being on even if the brakes have actually been serviced.


And that’s not all, as newer vehicles need to be put in a “service mode” to disengage the electronic parking brake before doing a brake job. Granted, there are hacks (involving a 12-volt battery and some wires) to release the parking brake from the rear discs, but the software still might block you from completing the service. Sometimes you have no choice but to visit the dealership to reset the system.


But as LaVar Burton from *Reading Rainbow* used to say, “you don’t have to take my word for it!”


The Car Wizard on YouTube said it well. Just because a good-hearted person like Adam helps his friends do their brakes, that isn’t a guarantee someone can complete the job on their (or Adam’s) driveway.


Look, as a former employee of one of the largest dealership groups on the planet, I am fine with putting OEM-branded walls around some issues. Any repair/service that’s free to the customer during the warranty period? Fine, make sure everyone goes back to the dealership. But if someone goes through brakes like it’s prime rib at a buffet, it needs to be extremely straightforward to reset the computer *and* disengage the parking brake.


I hope I am not acting like a wet blanket on Adam’s well-intentioned offer for his friends. Instead, I am encouraging him (and you!) to learn how to wrench, *and* to be engaged by ensuring we can still wrench in the future. We can do so by picking brands that don’t create hurdles to DIY and by supporting Right-to-Repair initiatives where you can.


Good luck, Adam. Your friends are lucky to have you in their lives. Now, it’s time for the Piston Slap community to sound off.
